## Graph construction and previously omitted small reads

A clean native ordinary-request diagnostic separates graph construction from
evaluation. It uses the same 15 GB ceiling, 4,067 slots, 8,192 context, BF16
activations/KV and FP32 recurrent state as the preceding work. Instrumented
requests are attribution evidence, not speed qualification.

Draft hidden-graph construction totals about 34/39 ms for code/prose. Expert
submission totals about 251/280 ms, of which 72/102 ms lies outside positive
read and GPU-encoder intervals. Parent and child scopes overlap. These scopes
do not justify a broad graph or reader port; they also do not prove that
overlapped work cannot affect the critical path or contend for memory.

The earlier read union omitted calls smaller than 64 KiB. Native Q2 embeddings
read a 1,100-byte compressed row per token ID, including repeated mask IDs in
each draft proposal. These are real reads, not host graph construction. The
graph diagnostic sees 1,478/1,609 such reads taking 179/120 ms in aggregate;
each request uses only 209 distinct offsets. PLE reads are smaller still but
almost entirely overlap other observed activity. Splash has no corresponding
1,100-byte embedding reads because it retains its prepared compressed table.
This is not evidence that retaining the whole table would earn its memory cost.

Counting all positive reads leaves about 1.130/1.141 seconds outside reads and
GPU encoders. Recorded host scopes cover 0.470/0.501 seconds of that interval.
The residual is about 0.660/0.640 seconds. These complements are elapsed
intervals, not pure CPU time or guaranteed removable delay.

## Per-lookup embedding deduplication is not retained

The first candidate reads each distinct token row once within an embedding
lookup and copies duplicate rows inside the same bounded output buffer. It
adds no persistent cache and changes no arithmetic or Fast path. The graph
trace identifies 672/810 duplicate mask reads within draft embedding calls,
with about 71/48 ms of read service. That is demonstrated redundant work,
not a predicted complete-request speedup.

Twenty-eight original-byte embedding comparisons pass across repeated,
mixed and unique IDs at 1, 2, 7, 8, 17, 64 and 512 rows. Three invalid-ID
refusals pass. An independent read observer sees exactly the expected 3,103
reference-plus-candidate row reads. The test helper's first build attempted
to access an internal property across modules; its geometry-based correction
and the failed build are preserved without changing the runtime candidate.

One frozen ABCCBA compares A=v68, B=dedup, C=published Splash 1.4.0. Every
fresh process uses two warmups and two timed 384-token code/prose requests,
normal adaptive verification and read-ahead, matched prompt IDs and actual
cache capacity. No read or GPU observers are injected into timed comparisons;
macmon is passive. All six arms pass memory, no-paging, nominal thermal and
no-competing-build gates.

| Task | Baseline median request s | Dedup median request s | Splash median request s | Dedup/baseline | Dedup/Splash |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Code | 12.271 | 11.760 | 11.169 | 0.9584 | 1.0529 |
| Prose | 13.318 | 13.310 | 12.541 | 0.9994 | 1.0614 |

Code improves in both order directions, but prose is flat in aggregate and
regresses about 1.30% in the reverse pair. It fails the preregistered

The second candidate starts again from v68. For Q2 greedy sampling with zero

Earlier ordinary traces identify 384 individual argmax boundaries per timed

Two hundred exact comparisons pass against the sequential sampler: FP32/BF16,

NaNs. Greedy RNG state is unchanged and unsupported settings fall back. The
short component process ends too quickly for its footprint sampler to capture

A second frozen ABCCBA, under the same complete-request contract, is clean in

| Task | Baseline median request s | Joint-greedy median request s | Splash median request s | Candidate/baseline | Candidate/Splash |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Code | 12.110 | 12.205 | 11.710 | 1.0079 | 1.0422 |
| Prose | 13.433 | 13.130 | 12.371 | 0.9774 | 1.0613 |

Prose improves in both directions, but code regresses in the forward pair and

## Dependency readiness does not establish the reader as the missing fix

Offline analysis joins each encoded host-ready wait to its publication and
the following measured GPU encoder. Internal waits use the preceding encoder
boundary. For first encoders, the lower boundary is the later of command
submission and the preceding observed GPU encoder end. Metal GPUStartTime can
follow publication and would incorrectly hide that queued dependency interval.
Upstream event pointer/value reuse is matched by publication time within the
owning command, not by assuming a globally unique pointer/value pair.

In the earlier clean copy-attribution pair, native has about 3.552/3.724 seconds
queued before readiness versus Splash's 4.468/4.980 seconds. Different adaptive
work and missing upstream encoder timestamps prevent a causal speed estimate.
The upstream pair omits 184 wait boundaries with missing stage timestamps;
other missing samples can widen uncovered intervals. After readiness, intervals
outside reads/encoders are about 0.106/0.111 seconds native and 0.101/0.123
seconds Splash. The named-trace pair gives the same qualitative result.

This does not show an excess native event-release delay or prove that all
reader scheduling is optimal. It weakens the case for rewriting the shared
reader from CPU wait sums, command counts or the previously observed fixed
probe alone. Useful overlap and actual dependency boundaries must be preserved.

## Narrowing the remaining unobserved regions

Offline localization of the graph diagnostic finds 0.263/0.268 seconds of
uncovered intervals between expert-demand preparation and the following MoE
return, and 0.206/0.213 seconds between the final target-layer tail and draft
context append. Adjacent scope names localize code regions; they are not
causal stacks or exclusive CPU attribution. The next diagnostic splits those
regions into demand reads/joins, promoted-ticket joining/adoption, publication,
target-call execution, logits evaluation, sampling and rollback.

The additional bounded diagnostic completes cleanly at a sampled physical
peak of 12.294 GB. It records the following code/prose scope totals. These
are native elapsed intervals; target-call scopes contain the smaller scopes
and cannot be added to them.

| Scope | Total elapsed s, code/prose | Outside reads/encoders s, code/prose |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Demand read function, including launch/join/copy/bookkeeping | 4.648 / 4.766 | 0.149 / 0.158 |
| Publish result and start next forecast | 0.114 / 0.124 | 0.085 / 0.093 |
| Join promoted forecasts | 0.009 / 0.008 | 0.002 / 0.002 |
| Adopt joined forecasts | 0.003 / 0.003 | 0.003 / 0.003 |
| Evaluate final logits | 0.251 / 0.280 | 0.022 / 0.025 |
| Sequential sampling loop | 0.084 / 0.086 | 0.068 / 0.070 |
| Rollback and reconcile before draft-context append | 0.055 / 0.057 | 0.053 / 0.054 |

The publication scope includes the `startForecast` callback, which ranks the
already computed forecast and expires/issues tickets. It must not be described
as event-signaling cost alone. Joining unfinished forecasts is too small here
to support an expensive shared-reader rewrite aimed at that join. The sampling
scope also limits what the rejected greedy-batching idea could remove.

The broader target-call scope contains about 0.475/0.534 seconds outside reads
and encoders, including its child preparation and demand scopes. Only about
0.138/0.123 seconds of the full requests remains outside all measured scopes,
reads and encoders. That is improved localization, not a removed delay.
Empty demand calls can have equal clock timestamps; the offline analyzer
accepts and counts those zero-duration scopes rather than rejecting valid
traces. No model rerun is used to repair that analysis assumption.

The next useful comparison is the demand-read lifecycle under the same real
verification work: separate launching/joining demand lanes, scratch copying,
metadata publication and concurrent forecast issue, with observer overhead
controlled. Current native scope totals alone do not establish an upstream
excess or justify another architecture port. Preserve the 15 GB baseline and
measure any narrowly justified change through complete requests.

## Limits and retained state

## Q2 demand lifecycle and buffer triage
Q2 parity remains unachieved. No runtime change is retained, and Fast stays
unchanged. These diagnostics follow [[records/measurements/q2-small-work-and-readiness]];
raw evidence is in [[sources/runs/2026/10/2026-10-25-q2-demand-lifecycle-triage]].

## Reader distribution does not yet justify a rewrite

The existing clean ordinary copy trace identifies all 77,754/80,910 code/prose
decode demand pieces. Unmatched raw copies equal exactly the prefill piece
counts and precede decode, where prefill uses CPU repacking. Every decoded
record has three unique pieces. All 4,718/4,928 batches validate against the
fixed-stride, same-thread lane order; no ambiguous groups are dropped.

For 637/652 batches with more jobs than lanes, the interval from the first
observed worker's last copy to the final read's start totals only
0.0573/0.0620 seconds. That is a conditional opportunity for stealing queued
work after an observed worker finishes, holding prior service fixed. It is
not a bound on every alternate scheduler, proof of worker idleness or a speed
prediction. It provides no evidence of a large benefit from replacing the pool.

A separate typical-route capture has consecutive missing-key group savings
of only 2.76%/2.23% before forecast adoption. Longest runs are three/four experts;
caps of eight or nine give identical counts. These are not actual demand jobs
or a bound on the fraction remaining after forecast adoption. Broad coalescing
is not justified by this count alone.

## Where readiness gaps occur

Decomposing previously matched native readiness windows gives about
0.026/0.026 seconds before the first observed read, 0.098/0.104 after the last,
and 0.002/0.002 between reads. Splash has about 0.096/0.107 before and
0.051/0.068 after. The source readiness analysis excludes missing upstream
encoder boundaries and records unequal adaptive work. All positive reads,
including unrelated forecasts, can overlap these windows. These temporal
positions are not exclusive CPU categories or causal speed estimates.
The longer native post-read portion is tens of milliseconds, not an established
explanation of the full request gap.

## Two small hypotheses checked

Both engines read the same original GGUF files. Native also requests
`F_RDAHEAD=0`; Splash leaves that flag at its default while both request
`F_NOCACHE=1`. An isolated native change enabling OS read-ahead compiles,
but a review of [Apple's published XNU read path](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/f6217f891ac0bb64f3d375211650a4c1ff8ca1ea/bsd/vfs/vfs_cluster.c#L4590)
weakens the mechanism: uncached reads select direct/contiguous I/O, and the
copy fallback suppresses read-ahead when `IO_NOCACHE` is set. The candidate
is abandoned before six expensive full-request arms. This source review is
not a measurement of the installed APFS implementation.

The other probe holds recorded offsets, read lengths, scratch pool, static
GCD lanes and copies constant while changing scratch allocation from aligned
ordinary RAM to shared Metal buffers. It replays the first 128 actual decode
demand batches, 2,814 reads and 1,342,773,248 requested bytes per round, without
GPU work or forecasts. Two warmups precede ABBA twice. Every batch's full
original-byte SHA-256 matches in all ten rounds, and paging does not change.

Median summed read/copy time is 0.130273 seconds with ordinary RAM and
0.130405 with Metal backing, a ratio of 1.0010. Paired directions vary. There
is no useful isolated gain worth adding another allocation policy. This does
not rule out a difference under concurrent GPU/forecast work. Hashing, original
interbatch gaps, metadata checks, adaptive control and model execution are
outside this narrow probe.

Both engines execute the same 84 prompt IDs and 111 sequential target passes:
472 target rows, widths one through eight, and 384 retained input tokens.
Every cycle computes a real seven-token draft proposal, runs the target on the
recorded inputs, computes greedy decisions and commits target/draft state using
the recorded accepted prefix. Only the choices of target inputs, width and
retention are frozen. Proposal computation is retained; it is not dummy work.

Each engine's 111 full-logit hashes and greedy IDs match its own prior target
reference. The two engines are not bit-identical to each other. All timing and
attribution passes also retain the validated real proposal IDs and selected
IDs. That establishes the diagnostic's target behavior, not semantic quality
of an ordinary generated answer or a quantization-loss bound.

Native uses v68 engine code with only the diagnostic CLI changed. Splash is

existing GPU copy operations save the actual proposals and impose fixed inputs,
width and retention without a new host wait. This diagnostic overhead and its
manual metadata finalization prevent equating it with the published executable.
No power manipulation, GPU spin or fake computation is introduced.

## Submission is a stronger lead than extra reader waiting

A separate native/Splash attribution pair repeats the same 111 full cycles with
bounded read/copy and named GPU-encoder observations. Both pass environmental
and selected-ID/proposal checks. Traced times are 11.195/10.930 seconds, compared

speed estimate. All native encoder samples are valid; 66 Splash encoder
boundaries are missing and remain counted.

| Observed full-cycle interval | Native s | Splash s |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Measured GPU encoder intervals | 5.735 | 6.417 |
| Queued dependency not yet published | 3.687 | 3.799 |
| After publication, before next encoder | 0.614 | 0.608 |
| GPU gap before next command submission | 0.912 | 0.069 |

Rows are different classifications and must not be added as independent
costs. Encoder intervals include stalls and scheduling, not pure instruction
execution. Missing samples can overstate gaps. The before-submission interval
identifies next work not yet submitted; it is not proof the CPU was running
throughout or that every millisecond can be removed.

About 0.677 seconds of native's pre-submission gaps fall in target verification,
0.142 in drafting, 0.028 in sampling and 0.064 in commit. Classifying the next
encoder locates 0.467 seconds before expert schedules. Only 0.034 seconds precede
encoders containing the final combine. Moving that combine earlier therefore
has a small observed scope and does not justify reviving the rejected
forecast-launch candidate. Cache claims, routing readback and preparation
before submission remain the stronger region to isolate.

Native's 78,891 attributed demand copies exactly match three copies per fetched
expert. Copies overlap reads/GPU work; their union outside both is 0.072 seconds.
The larger parallel copy service sum is not removable request delay. Likewise,
more demand records do not establish a larger exposed read wait: native's
matched queued-readiness interval is slightly shorter here. Neither this trace
nor CPU wait sums justify a shared-reader rewrite.

identify a larger bounded contribution outside the already measured wrappers,
or demonstrate a materially different execution dependency. Do not continue
with low-ceiling changes because their source resembles Splash. Retain the
published Splash baseline and require repeatable complete requests before any
performance claim. No new ordinary native/Splash comparison is warranted for
these rejected or unqualified candidates.

## What differs from Splash

Splash revision `1482f6bbc2abf12375332725302019594150b6cb` uses a shared reader
pool. At demand, it halts unclaimed forecast tasks, preserves already started
pieces and reads only the remaining pieces through foreground scheduling.
Native uses separate demand lanes and four ordered forecast queues. It already
cancels wrong predictions before demand and promotes forecasts with completed
pieces. However, its `claimSplit` discards a ticket with zero completed pieces
even when a checked read has already started. Cancellation can discard that
read before its bytes are copied, then demand reads the same piece again.

A copy-only trace misses this work. Match every successful expert pread to its
exact original GGUF tensor, row and projection, then match forecast and demand
within the same verification cycle. The corrected parser maps every large read
and reconciles demand pieces exactly to three times the fetched-record count.

| Trace | Demand pieces | Forecast pieces | Duplicate pieces | Affected records |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Prior full-cycle baseline | 78,891 | 109,516 | 4,387 | 2,596 |
| Prior submission probe | 78,075 | 110,740 | 4,314 | 2,566 |
| Started-forecast candidate | 70,581 | 113,786 | 0 | 0 |

These are separate instrumented executions, not identical timing samples.
Same-cycle matching is the stated scope; it is not a proof about arbitrary
cross-cycle duplication. Forecast-reader classification is checked against the
exact demand total. The candidate trace preserves all 111 proposals and selected
token lists from its separate exact validation.

The original duplicated demand reads have about 2.13/2.17 seconds of summed
service and 1.26/1.28 seconds of interval union. Neither measures recoverable
request time. Holding every other completion fixed and replacing duplicates
with their earlier forecast completion advances the last demand completion by
only 15.8/13.1 milliseconds across the whole trace. Those intervals are outside
observed GPU encoders, but publication and other dependencies can still dominate.
This argues against a broad scheduler rewrite based on duplicate-read sums.
It does not measure the indirect contention effect of avoiding the reads.

## Reusing a fixed draft mask

Native Q2 reads and decodes the anchor plus seven identical mask rows on every
draft proposal. The earlier per-lookup read deduplication still decoded all
eight rows and was rejected. This different candidate retains one decoded
BF16 mask row inside its immutable checkpoint, reads/decodes only the anchor,
and broadcasts/concatenates the mask into the original eight-row block. Fast
and non-Q2 lookups keep the original expression. There is no reader, controller,
expert-cache or arithmetic change.

The persistent payload is 5,120 bytes, with an additional 16 KiB planner reserve.
Clearing embedding storage releases the cached owner; a different checkpoint
has independent state. The diagnostic tests 18 exact original-row cases,
changing masks and anchors, clear/reload and four invalid IDs. All pass.
All 111 full-logit hashes, real proposals and selected tokens match the frozen
native reference. Validation retains 4,067 slots and passes its 15 GB ceiling.

The synchronous 512-lookup component control takes 0.312/0.309 s baseline and
0.111/0.105 s candidate under Metal API validation. That proves a local effect
in that diagnostic, not a complete-request improvement. Extra tensor assembly
and changed execution timing still have to earn their complexity in production.

## Q2 early expert preparation: exact but not faster
Preparing Q2 expert work before the required router readback preserves tested arithmetic, but this implementation fails its clean speed gate. It is not retained. ## One bounded scheduling change

The existing path waits for route IDs, then prepares and submits the expert job. The candidate prepares and submits a gated expert job while the already-submitted router runs. After the router finishes, it binds actual grouping, pool slots and staging destinations, performs the same required reads and publishes the same readiness event. It changes no reader count, cache policy, arithmetic, worker pool, polling or GPU power policy.

Unknown routes require bounded maximum-capacity metadata and padded output rows. Inactive expert tiles return without matrix arithmetic; the fixed final tile holds the shared expert. This can still add gathering, dispatch and allocation work, so equal arithmetic is not a speed argument. Only the eligible Q2 mixed path enters; deferred readback arrays and unavailable staging capacity fall back to the existing path.

The early job must share the existing 110,592,000-byte raw staging reserve with every still-live previous raw allocation. Reservations follow actual MLX data owners through GPU completion, not merely the Swift ticket's scope. Failure, cancellation or unavailable capacity cannot acquire a second reserve. Forecasts still do not select victims or change cache ownership.

Additional cases cover unbound publication, repeated cancellation, invalid routes, duplicate staging destinations, rebinding, temporary tensor owners, one/two/eight input rows and reservation refusal. All pass under Metal validation. The small safety process peaks at 0.701 GB with no paging.

It takes the early path 3,860 times and refuses 1,357 times for the existing staging limit; the final live reservation is zero. This establishes actual branch execution and arithmetic equivalence for these fixtures, not semantic task quality or release readiness.

## Fast boundary correction and final state

An earlier caveat in the two linked forecast records incorrectly required a new Q2-only metadata allocation boundary. Both Swift and C++ already reject nonempty staging for affine/Fast plans, and Job.prepare_staging returns for zero count before allocating source metadata. The four-int allocation is thus already restricted to the staged non-affine path. The frozen original clarification remains in the archive; the new source audit corrects the derived conclusion. Do not add an unnecessary isolation patch or count this audit as a new Fast performance test.

All 509 runtime inputs and five default v68 artifacts are restored. No optimization, release or Smart promotion is retained. Existing Fast recall and Q2 strict-format failures remain separate from these timing/functional checks; full application readiness is not established.

## Q2 runtime row counts remove repeated compilation; first-request qualification stays open
A small Q2 change removes redundant Metal program creation and improves warmed complete requests against copy-only in both orders. Warmed code and prose stay within 0.4 percent of published Splash. The first request still varies from 23.2178 to 12.5747 seconds, however, and the slower one regresses against native v68. The frozen retention and all-request parity gates fail. Preserve the tested candidate in the evidence archive, keep production v68 and Fast unchanged, and continue investigating first-request preparation.

This follows [[records/measurements/q2-adaptive-decisions-and-preparation]]. The earlier prepared-cycle cost omission remains rejected. Evidence is [[sources/runs/2026/10/2026-10-26-q2-cold-compilation-and-row-counts]]. All new complete-request arms are clean; a favorable later launch does not replace the slow first one.

## Fix the workload before assigning a cause

Capture one actual 384-token first request with the bounded decision trace and a synchronous Metal library/pipeline creation observer. Select the first 24 verification passes by ordinal before inspecting their timing. The captured first request takes 24.3927 seconds, uses 217 passes including 148 anchor-only passes, and creates 160 source libraries and 196 pipeline states during the request. Its creation calls contain 7.0929 seconds of CPU wall time. This is instrumented diagnostic evidence, not a product-speed measurement or seven seconds of proven GPU idleness.

The captured widths start at eight, three, two and one, then remain at one through the 24-pass fixture. The existing native-projection preparation flag marks only the first pass. New custom-kernel compilation continues at later widths after that flag clears. Omitting one entire flagged cost sample therefore does not establish that recurring cost learning is free of later preparation.

For native v68, copy-only and pinned source Splash 1482f6b, retire forecasts and clear only expert residency before each of three rounds. Preserve allocated slots. Re-prefill the same 84 tokens and execute the frozen inputs, widths and retained prefixes with real seven-token drafting, target evaluation, greedy selection and rollback/commit. Do not reset OS file caches, compiler caches or embedding/PLE caches. Native uses an 8,192-token context reservation; source uses the existing bounded fixture arena. This is a controlled execution diagnostic, not a claim of identical complete-process reservations.

Native baseline and copy-only match every full logit, actual proposal and selected token across all rounds and against each other. Native repeats exactly 3,882 logical required misses per round; source repeats 3,879. Prefill reads are 7,785 and 7,783 respectively. Cross-engine arithmetic/routes are close but not bit-identical. Demand versus adopted reads can differ while required logical misses remain fixed.

## Observe preparation without equating CPU wait with GPU idle

The bounded observer wraps the original synchronous Metal calls once, leaves their arguments and ownership unchanged, and serializes only at process exit. A genuine small-kernel self-check validates all three hooks and exact output. No GPU keepalive, priority/power change, per-read tracing or GPU counter injection is used.

An off/on/on/off same-binary fixed-work control preserves actual proposals and selected IDs. All four arms are clean; every forward/reverse round ratio stays within two percent. Pooled differences are +0.29, -0.82 and +0.68 percent. This qualifies the observer in that control; it does not make arbitrary compiler-cache states identical.

All six A/B/S/S/B/A fixed timing arms are clean. First-round 24-pass times are 2.4835/2.5351 seconds for native, 2.4290/1.5931 for copy-only and 1.4868/1.4081 for source. Later rounds contain no creation calls during these passes. Native/copy first-round creation-call unions vary from 0.0171 to 0.8119 seconds; source creates pipeline states from existing libraries in about 0.0021–0.0023 seconds and compiles no source library inside the fixture. The same logical misses recur, while startup preparation and its timing vary.

Creation-call unions are CPU intervals and can overlap useful GPU work or reads. They must not be subtracted and labeled an exact exposed bottleneck. The capture's larger request-wide compilation cost also cannot be substituted for the fixed replay. This evidence supports targeting one-time program creation, without proving that every remaining delay is compilation or justifying a shared-reader rewrite.

## One small implementation change

Three Q2 kernels specialize a token count that does not define different arithmetic: GGUF embedding decode, PLE convolution and Q/K preparation. Pass their counts through the existing Metal grid size or input-shape metadata. Keep format, precision, dimensions defining the arithmetic, memory limits, sampler and adaptive policy unchanged. This adds no performance switch or alternate backend.

The isolated candidate combines those three changes with the same seven-file aligned forecast implementation used by copy-only. Diagnostic CLI additions do not enter the product path. The baseline and copy-only remain independent controls.

Each affected family creates five pipelines in the baseline fixture: one for prefill and four during verification. The candidate creates one at prefill and none during any verification round. This confirms the intended mechanism rather than inferring it from throughput.

Expanded independent checks pass for every admitted format, FP32/BF16 partial decoded prefixes including non-threadgroup-aligned counts, attention widths one through nine plus 33/84/129 with two batches, and the existing FP64 PLE oracle and all 32 rollback cuts. Native scheduling, packed bytes, lifecycle and affine checks also pass. The candidate's 72 real-model frozen passes match the baseline's full logits, proposals and selected IDs exactly. These are arithmetic/state checks, not semantic task-quality qualification.

## Complete requests decide retention

Freeze A/B/C/S/S/C/B/A before collecting candidate results. A is native v68, B copy-only, C copy plus runtime counts, and S published Splash 1.4.0. Each fresh process executes two warmups and then code/prose requests, all 384 output tokens, with original prompt IDs, 4,067 actual slots, 15 GB physical ceilings, BF16 activations/KV, FP32 recurrence and an 8,192-token requested context. Admit only with at least 18 GB reclaimable and preserve at least 1 GB headroom. Hold one global reservation across the protocol. No compilation observer runs during these requests.

All eight arms finish cleanly. Every result remains included. Values are forward / reverse complete-request seconds after model loading, including prefill. They do not include model preparation or establish full application-launch latency.

| Engine | First request | Second request | Warmed code | Warmed prose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Native v68 | 19.7537 / 20.4063 | 13.3548 / 14.3691 | 12.8632 / 12.9072 | 14.1012 / 13.9861 |
| Copy-only | 26.5598 / 22.4430 | 13.5594 / 13.2529 | 12.4274 / 12.8138 | 13.3972 / 14.6003 |
| Copy + runtime counts | 23.2178 / 12.5747 | 13.5457 / 13.1733 | 11.8357 / 12.4073 | 13.0044 / 13.0905 |
| Published Splash | 12.1795 / 12.4466 | 13.0093 / 14.4499 | 12.0093 / 12.3606 | 13.0416 / 13.2373 |

C improves warmed code against B by 4.76/3.17 percent and prose by 2.93/10.34 percent. Against Splash, code is 1.45 percent faster / 0.38 percent slower, and prose 0.29/1.11 percent faster. The second request is also within five percent of Splash in both orders. These are repeatable warmed results for these tasks, not a general hardware or model-quality claim.

The first request improves against B by 12.58/43.97 percent, but the forward C request is 17.54 percent slower than A and 90.63 percent slower than S. Reverse C is only 1.03 percent slower than S. Its first-request prefill changes from 5.1020 to 1.3170 seconds and verification work from 215 passes to 110. Preserve this variation; do not select only the fast launch or claim complete-request parity.

The predeclared retention rule required both-order first-request improvement against copy-only, no material regression against native, and no material later regression. The first native comparison fails it. The all-request Splash gate fails too. No production optimization is retained in this checkpoint, despite the verified mechanism and warmed wins. The isolated source and executable identity remain available for the next targeted experiment.

## Next action and limits

Profile the remaining library creation in the ordinary first prefill and first verification pass, recording source hashes and compile options as well as names. Compare those identities with the fixed replay to distinguish genuine new programs from compiler-cache variation. Establish which preparation can be reused before the engine reports ready or supplied as compiled Metal libraries before making a larger change. Any such test must include model preparation plus the first request: merely moving work outside the request timer is not a speedup.

Do not repeat broad porting, reset calibration, force widths or revive the rejected cost omission on this evidence alone. Preserve Fast's established performance path. Known Fast recall and Q2 strict-format failures remain tracked separately. All 509 runtime inputs, five default v68 artifacts and dependency bytes/modes are restored, and no release, Smart promotion or full app-readiness claim is made.

## Q2 compilation spikes isolated; offline treatment does not earn integration
The offline-compilation experiment removes a real first-use cost, but it does not earn production integration. It fails the frozen repeatability and complete-request gates. Keep native v68, preserve Fast's qualified execution path, and keep Q2 outside the Smart alias. Matching another implementation is useful only when it improves completed work with acceptable quality and maintenance cost.

This follows [[records/measurements/q2-cold-compilation-and-row-counts]]. Evidence is [[sources/runs/2026/10/2026-10-26-q2-compiler-and-workflow-checkpoint]]. The bounded Fast recall diagnosis is recorded separately in [[records/measurements/relevant-conversation-excerpts]].

## What compilation identity proves

Record exact source hashes, compile options and device metadata around the original Metal calls. Common sets of identical requested programs can take about seven seconds in one launch and about fifty milliseconds in another. The three runtime-count kernels do not account for most of that variation. A small executable/copy comparison does not establish executable identity as the compiler-cache cause. Do not replace the unresolved OS compiler-cache behavior with a claimed explanation.

The observer's first-round off/on/on/off sensitivity control fails, although its later rounds pass. Consequently, the instrumented ordinary runs are causal diagnostics, not uninstrumented production qualification. Metadata collection itself is small, but that does not rescue a failed sensitivity gate. Compilation call durations can overlap expert reads and GPU execution; their CPU wall time is not proven GPU idle time.

## Full-model correctness constrains offline compilation

The isolated manual CI experiment compiles the captured source and options with the available Xcode toolchain. All 174 libraries compile, but substituting the whole set fails the frozen full-model comparison: all 72 logit hashes differ, with 45 proposal-array and 12 selected-array mismatches. The JIT control on the same candidate matches the reference exactly.

Group isolation locates the tested mismatch in a pair of shared steel attention/GEMM libraries. Other tested groups match, but this does not identify the precise compiler transformation or establish harmless numerical drift. Small kernel checks had passed; they were insufficient to validate the combined model.

A narrower treatment substitutes only 123 Q2-specific libraries: 35 resident projection programs and 88 custom Q2/GGUF programs. Shared MLX and Fast kernels remain JIT-compiled. Three rounds of the frozen 24-pass fixture preserve every full-logit hash, actual draft proposal and selected token. This establishes exactness on those inputs, not broad semantic quality or negligible Q2 quantization loss. The compiled libraries, source/options, compiler provenance and failed treatments are preserved in the archive.

## One complete-request comparison

Freeze A/B/C/S/S/C/B/A before execution. A is production native v68, B is the previous isolated aligned-forecast/runtime-count candidate, C is the same B executable with the Q2-only offline treatment, and S is published Splash. All native arms use the same observer/loader, with an empty replacement directory for A/B. No production injection or compiled-library loading path is introduced.

Match exact prompt IDs, 4,067 expert slots, a 15 GB physical ceiling, an 8,192-token context reservation, BF16 activations/KV and FP32 recurrence. Each fresh process executes first and second requests followed by warmed coding and prose, with 384 generated tokens each. Reserve the machine for the whole protocol, require 18 GB reclaimable before each arm, preserve 1 GB headroom, and retain all arms. No compiler-cache or file-cache purge is performed.

All eight arms finish without the timing protocol's paging, competing-build or thermal exclusions. These values are complete-request seconds after loading, forward / reverse order:

| Engine | First request | Second request | Warmed code | Warmed prose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Native v68 | 13.0975 / 20.8006 | 13.6823 / 14.0445 | 13.2381 / 13.2203 | 14.3007 / 13.6803 |
| Runtime-count candidate | 21.7248 / 13.7294 | 13.9365 / 13.3658 | 12.8693 / 14.2830 | 13.6444 / 13.9505 |
| Candidate + Q2-only offline libraries | 12.7801 / 13.6440 | 13.5353 / 13.5358 | 13.1342 / 13.0852 | 13.0230 / 12.9910 |
| Published Splash | 11.9964 / 13.8150 | 13.1246 / 16.1420 | 11.3127 / 12.2660 | 12.9714 / 15.9506 |

C passes the no-regression comparison against A. Against B, its first-request improvement is about 41 percent forward and less than one percent reverse, so the predeclared repeatable five-percent benefit fails. Forward warmed code also slightly exceeds the two-percent no-regression limit. Against Splash, warmed code remains about 16.1 and 6.7 percent slower. The first forward request also exceeds the five-percent parity limit. All-request parity and retention both fail; no favorable subset replaces that verdict.

Offline treatment reduces total source-library creation call time to about 0.042 seconds in both C processes, versus 4.567 and 0.055 seconds in B. This supports compilation as a source of spikes, while ruling out its removal as a sufficient solution to the remaining gap. Adaptive scheduling and actual speculative work can differ when costs change; these complete requests are the product outcome, not equal fixed verification work.

The earlier interrupted protocol is separately excluded in full. Its sole completed arm recorded paging, and the owning turn ended before the remaining arms. The verified orphan telemetry process was stopped. Its files remain intact; the subsequent complete protocol was frozen independently and includes every new arm.

## The next useful target

Model loading is consistently about 29 seconds natively versus about seven seconds in Splash in this study. Loading plus the first response is roughly 42–51 seconds for native and 19–21 seconds for Splash. These measured process intervals are not full GUI launch measurements, and the instrumentation qualification limit still applies.

Code inspection shows that native Q2 loading authenticates the complete pinned checkpoint with SHA-256 on each open, before parsing and resident preparation. That is a concrete startup hypothesis, not measured phase attribution. Profile authentication, parsing/conversion, allocation and GPU preparation separately before changing startup. Preserve pinned-byte authentication, cancellation and mutation detection; removing verification is not a valid shortcut to parity.

Keep the isolated compiler workflow as reproducible experimental tooling. Do not add a production loader, prewarming pass, cache override, broad scheduler rewrite or Fast engine change on this evidence. Reopen the offline approach only after exact full-model validation and a repeatable improvement in loading plus complete first and subsequent responses. Existing strict-format and semantic quality failures remain separate gates.

## Relevant conversation excerpts repair tested factual recall; citation quality remains open
A bounded app context change repairs the tested Fast factual-recall failure without changing either model's execution path. When a question matches an older message, automatic excerpts now prefer that evidence over unrelated recent fragments. The original question returns the correct workshop code with DFlash enabled and disabled, and across Fast to Q2 to Fast switching. Unsupported citation markers remain an explicit output-quality issue; this is not full app-readiness qualification.

Evidence is [[sources/runs/2026/10/2026-10-26-q2-compiler-and-workflow-checkpoint]]. This addresses the app failures preserved in [[records/measurements/native-prepared-execution]], separately from the Q2 performance experiment in [[records/measurements/q2-compiler-identity-and-precompiled-shaders]].

## Diagnose before changing the model

The original v68 app fixture stores a workshop code in its oldest message, followed by sixty repetitive unrelated messages. The app keeps a complete recent window and a small set of older excerpts. Previously those excerpts came only from the most recent omitted messages, without considering the question. The correct old fact therefore was not supplied initially, and Fast did not call history.search. It repeated the unrelated conversation pattern instead.

Freeze the original app/check/helper identities and repeat the original writing/admitted-memory setup plus the unchanged history question on disposable Homes. Both normal drafting and target-only decoding fail factual recall with the same unrelated repetition. This reduced control isolates a failure that is not specific to DFlash; it is not a replay of every original app job or a new engine-speed comparison.

## Small shared retrieval change

Reuse the lexical word-overlap ranking already used for saved memories. Within the existing permitted conversation, score omitted messages against the current question; recency breaks ties and selected excerpts render in chronological order. Preserve the existing complete-message window, maximum number and size of excerpts, quoted-data label, exact message IDs, and context receipt.

Automatic scanning shares Recall's existing allowance of at most 512 records and one MiB of text. An old message that cannot fit the remaining scan allowance is skipped; paginated history.search remains available for older or larger material. These are work bounds, not measured semantic-recall optima. No synonym model, embedding dependency, new performance knob, task-specific phrase or model prompt is added.

Start an excerpt near a matching word rather than always at the message opening. Keep its existing 240-character and 320-byte maximum, with at most 80 bytes of preceding context. A newly added test first reproduced how an 80-character lookbehind could consume the whole byte allowance with emoji and discard the matching fact. Bounding that lookbehind by bytes, while retaining complete characters, fixes the test. This does not guarantee that every relevant fact fits in one excerpt.

Forget filtering and conversation boundaries apply before ranking. Scripted tests cover a fact beyond both the recent window and the opening of a long message, multibyte text, a different question selecting different evidence, quoted provenance, Forget, and a separate Incognito conversation receiving none of the original thread's facts.

## Qualification and remaining failures

The complete native scripted app suite passes. The later Unicode edge-case check fails before its correction and passes afterward. All raw results and both candidate versions remain preserved.

The final real-model replay runs the original six workflow categories with normal Fast: writing, PDF evidence, receipt JSON, CSV calculation, reviewed code editing and history recall. It then changes the loaded model to Q2 and back to Fast on the same conversation. A separate target-only control repeats writing and recall. All ten jobs pass their mechanical workflow checks, including actual model identity, startup recipe, native execution, explicit memory ceiling, successful terminal state and exact approved code change. The final process-footprint values are in the linked receipt. Each arm stays inside its 10 GB functional budget on the 48 GB development Mac. This is not physical 16/64 GB hardware qualification or new clean speed evidence.

The recall assertion now accepts either history.search evidence or an initially selected excerpt bound to the original message ID. The user question and required code are unchanged. Requiring a search call after the correct evidence has already been supplied would test a particular route instead of the person's task. Earlier failures are retained and are not reclassified as successes.

Manual output review still finds an unsupported literal [S1] in the history and model-switch answers, with no source excerpts in those jobs. The renderer leaves unknown citation markers unlinked; it does not borrow another job's source. The correct code is supported by inspectable conversation evidence, but the invented marker is an open model-output defect. The final code-edit explanation is also longer than the requested single sentence despite proposing the correct reviewed edit. Preserve those exact answers for separate output-quality corrections rather than broadening citation ownership or silently treating an invented marker as evidence.

The development app bundle is rebuilt and ad-hoc signature-verified against the same source inputs used by the final real-model checks. Production engine sources and the default v68 engine artifacts remain unchanged. Keep prior strict-format and semantic-quality failures open, keep Q2 an explicit candidate, and make no release or general-readiness claim from these tests.

## PR hardening: first integrated baseline comparison
The first 45 reviewed PRs were built together and compared with the original pre-review baseline on the same 48 GB M5 Pro. [[sources/runs/2026/11/2026-11-04-pr-baseline-vs-45-merged]] preserves the raw twelve-process experiment and binary identities.

The original commit is `c0c55d86866d77ae7fc2bf7b57b1c0faf7f9df25`. The comparison is main `d566a418bf41d5d41c92c218220f917c1a7fb575`, tree `702becbf8e6930e014a98c2141b1b3b2b3926d36`. Each arm has its own release executable and the same pinned metallib. Fresh processes start with empty expert and prefix caches; filesystem caching is uncontrolled and not purged.

Three interleaved paired rounds for each short/prose fixture use an 8.1 GB target, 256-token passes, greedy output, seed 7, MTP off and 32 generated tokens. Every paired output-ID list is identical. All twelve cells are eligible, with no excluded or swapping round. Median paired complete-request reductions are 1.47% for short and 1.41% for prose. These small differences do not establish a general speed improvement; they show no meaningful slowdown in these bounded cases.

This comparison does not qualify all prompts, longer contexts, MTP, clients, power conditions or the full 16–64 GB target range. It does not adopt a new default optimization. The remaining engine PRs and validation corrections are qualified separately before integration.
